query: FCC high-entropy alloys lose substantial strength above 800 °C, motivating refractory high-entropy alloys. Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW retains excellent mechanical properties at 1600 °C but has poor room-temperature ductility, and its irradiation resistance has been inferred computationally rather than established here experimentally. Studies of other refractory high-entropy alloys have found greater irradiation resistance than pure tungsten under helium implantation and self-healing behavior associated with enhanced atomic diffusion and redistribution. However, irradiation-induced amorphization, helium-energy-dependent blistering, and irradiation-enhanced precipitation have also been observed, indicating unresolved phase- and surface-stability risks. Given the need to preserve BCC structural stability and high-temperature mechanical performance while improving room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance, what intervention could achieve this balance? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted directional or quantitative outcomes relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the applicable temperature and irradiation boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Minor Ti addition and controlled aging in NbMoTaW will form coherent Ti-rich B2 nanoprecipitates that act as defect sinks and dislocation-facilitating interfaces, thereby increasing room-temperature ductility and irradiation tolerance without compromising high-temperature strength.
generation.material_initial_state: Equal-atomic, single-phase BCC NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy, as-cast and homogenized.
generation.intervention: Alloy with 2 at% Ti and perform aging heat treatment at 1000 °C for 10 h.
generation.conditions: Aging at 1000 °C/10 h; mechanical testing at 300 K and 1600 °C; He-ion irradiation to 5 dpa at 600 °C.
generation.structural_mediator: Coherent Ti-rich B2 nanoprecipitates (∼10–20 nm) uniformly dispersed in the BCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: Precipitates provide efficient sinks for radiation defects, reducing void swelling and loop density, and their coherent interfaces lower the stress barrier for dislocation nucleation and motion at low temperature; the solid-solution matrix plus stable precipitates retain high-temperature strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to untreated NbMoTaW, the Ti-alloyed aged alloy will show ~30% higher tensile elongation at 300 K, equal or higher yield strength at 300 K, ≥90% retention of yield strength at 1600 °C, and ≥40% reduction in void swelling and dislocation-loop density under 5 dpa He irradiation at 600 °C.
generation.baseline: Untreated NbMoTaW: <10% elongation at 300 K, yield strength ≈1300 MPa at 1600 °C, high void swelling and loop densities under 5 dpa He irradiation.
generation.boundary: Benefits expected between 300 K–800 °C and up to 5 dpa He; precipitate coarsening may reduce ductility gains above 1200 °C; effectiveness uncertain above 10 dpa.
generation.uncertainty: Exact magnitude of ductility improvement and irradiation tolerance enhancement is uncertain due to lack of prior data on Ti in NbMoTaW and precipitate stability at extreme temperatures.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize NbMoTaW+2 at% Ti, age at 1000 °C for 10 h. Confirm nanoprecipitate size/distribution by TEM. Perform tensile tests at 300 K and 1600 °C. Irradiate to 5 dpa He at 600 °C. Measure tensile elongation, yield strength, void swelling, dislocation-loop density.
measurements: room-temperature tensile elongation and yield strength
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: Hypothesis is falsified if Ti-alloyed aged alloy fails to exhibit ≥20% increase in 300 K elongation, or shows >10% drop in 1600 °C yield strength, or fails to reduce void swelling by ≥20% under the specified irradiation.
